typing-speed-test.title: Typing speed test
typing-speed-test.desc: Measure your typing speed in words per minute and your accuracy against a fixed sample, with the formula and a running timer shown.
typing-speed-test.lede: Type the sample text below. The clock starts on your first keystroke and stops when you press Finish; you get words per minute, accuracy and the arithmetic behind both.
typing-speed-test.how: Words per minute here uses the five-character convention: WPM = correct characters ÷ 5 ÷ minutes elapsed. A character counts as correct when your text matches the sample at that position, so a typo costs one character even if the rest lines up. Accuracy = correct characters ÷ characters typed × 100. The clock uses the browser's high-resolution timer and starts on the first keystroke rather than on a button, so the result includes the time spent reading the sample. Nothing is recorded: no history, no cookies, no local storage, so reloading the page clears the attempt. The samples are built in and short enough to finish in well under a minute at an ordinary speed.
typing-speed-test.example: Typing 250 characters in exactly one minute with 25 of them wrong leaves 225 correct. That is 225 ÷ 5 ÷ 1 = 45 words per minute, with 225 ÷ 250 = 90% accuracy. The same 225 characters typed in 30 seconds would read as 90 WPM, because half the time means twice the rate.

faq.q: Why five characters per word?
faq.a: It is the long-standing typing convention: it treats a word plus the space after it as five characters, so spaces and punctuation count. A five-letter word typed with a trailing space is one word for this measurement.

faq.q: Does fixing a typo count as correct?
faq.a: Yes. The comparison uses the final text in the box, position by position, so a corrected character counts as correct. The time you spent fixing it still counts against you, which is why accuracy and speed are reported separately.

faq.q: What if I stop before the end?
faq.a: Finish uses whatever you have typed. Accuracy then compares against only those characters, and WPM counts the correct ones. An attempt shorter than a sentence is not a useful measurement.

faq.q: Are my results stored or compared with anyone?
faq.a: No. There is no account, no leaderboard and no storage of any kind. The numbers exist in the page until you reload it or type again.

faq.q: How accurate is a very short attempt?
faq.a: Short attempts are noisy because the rate is extrapolated to a full minute. A few seconds of typing can read as several hundred WPM. Type for at least 20 to 30 seconds if you want a figure that means something.

regex-tester.title: Regex tester
regex-tester.desc: Test a JavaScript regular expression against your own text and see every match, capture group and position, with flags and clear errors for invalid patterns.
regex-tester.lede: Enter a pattern, choose flags and paste the text to search. The tool lists each match with its position and capture groups, and explains any pattern that will not compile.
regex-tester.how: The pattern is compiled with the RegExp constructor, which is the same engine your browser runs at run time, not a lookalike written for this page. Flags are passed as written: g finds every match, i ignores case, m makes ^ and $ match line ends, s lets a dot match newlines and u enables Unicode mode. Each match is reported with its start and end index plus its text. Capture groups are numbered in the order their opening bracket appears, and named groups are shown under their name. The tool stops after 1,000 matches so a broad pattern cannot hang the tab, and it refuses patterns that nest a quantifier inside a quantified group, such as (a+)+, because those can backtrack exponentially.
regex-tester.example: With the pattern \b(\w+)@(\w+)\.com\b and the g flag, the text "ann@example.com and bo@test.com" gives two matches. Match 1 is ann@example.com at indices 0 to 15, with group 1 ann and group 2 example. Match 2 is bo@test.com at indices 20 to 31, with groups bo and test.

faq.q: Which regular-expression flavour is this?
faq.a: JavaScript, exactly as your browser implements it. That includes named groups, lookahead, lookbehind and Unicode property escapes in current browsers. PCRE-only syntax such as recursion or branch-reset groups is not available.

faq.q: Why was my pattern refused?
faq.a: Two guards. A pattern longer than 300 characters is refused, and so is one that puts a quantifier inside an already quantified group, because that shape can take exponential time on a hostile input. The message names the reason.

faq.q: Do matches update while I type?
faq.a: Yes. Every change to the pattern, the flags or the text re-runs the match and replaces the list. Invalid patterns show the engine's error message instead of matches.

faq.q: Why does ^ not match the start of every line?
faq.a: Without the m flag, ^ and $ mean the start and end of the whole string. Turn on m to make them match around line breaks, which is what most multi-line text needs.

faq.q: Is the text I paste uploaded?
faq.a: No. Matching happens in this tab and nothing is sent. There is no history, so the pattern and text disappear when you reload.

hash-generator.title: Hash generator
hash-generator.desc: Create a SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512 hash of any text using your browser's Web Crypto API. The text never leaves the page.
hash-generator.lede: Paste text, choose an algorithm and get the hex digest. Hashing uses the browser's built-in Web Crypto implementation, so nothing is sent anywhere.
hash-generator.how: A hash function turns any input into a fixed-length fingerprint. This page calls crypto.subtle.digest over the UTF-8 bytes of your text. SHA-256 always returns 32 bytes, SHA-512 returns 64, SHA-384 returns 48 and SHA-1 returns 20, each printed as two hex digits per byte. Hashing is one-way: you can confirm a suspected input by hashing it again, but you cannot recover the original text from the digest. The same input always produces the same output, and changing one character produces a completely different one. MD5 is deliberately absent, because it is broken for collision resistance and Web Crypto does not expose it. Input is capped at 100,000 characters so the page stays responsive on a slow device.
hash-generator.example: The SHA-256 digest of the text abc is ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad, which is 64 hex characters. The SHA-1 digest of the same three characters is a9993e364706816aba3e25717850c26c9cd0d89d, only 40 characters, so the algorithm matters when you compare two digests.

faq.q: Can I hash a file here?
faq.a: No. This tool hashes text. A file tool would need to read the bytes of the file, and the page does not offer that, so paste text instead or use a dedicated file-checksum tool.

faq.q: Can a hash be reversed?
faq.a: Not in practice. The digest does not contain the input, and many different inputs can exist in theory, which is why a hash confirms an input rather than revealing it.

faq.q: Why is MD5 missing?
faq.a: MD5 is not collision resistant: different inputs can be crafted to share a digest. Web Crypto does not offer it either, so this page could not run it without a custom implementation.

faq.q: Should I use this for passwords?
faq.a: No. A single fast hash is the wrong tool for passwords. Password storage needs a deliberately slow, salted algorithm such as Argon2, scrypt or bcrypt, and that is a server-side design decision.

faq.q: Why does an empty box show a message?
faq.a: Empty input does have a valid digest, but a message makes it clear that nothing was hashed. Paste or type text first and the digest appears as you type.

lorem-ipsum-generator.title: Lorem ipsum generator
lorem-ipsum-generator.desc: Generate placeholder text as paragraphs, sentences or single words from a built-in word list, with a chosen amount and the option to start with Lorem ipsum.
lorem-ipsum-generator.lede: Choose paragraphs, sentences or words, set how many, and copy the placeholder text. Everything is generated in your browser from a fixed word list.
lorem-ipsum-generator.how: The generator draws words from a built-in list of sixty-three Latin-looking words and assembles them into sentences and paragraphs. Sentence mode returns exactly the number you ask for, paragraph mode groups three to five sentences per paragraph, and word mode returns the count directly. The first word of each sentence is capitalised and the sentence ends with a full stop, so the output reads as prose. With the lorem-ipsum switch on, the text begins with the traditional opening instead of a random word. Counts are capped at 10 paragraphs, 30 sentences and 200 words, which keeps the page responsive. There is no network request and no history: the text exists only in this tab until you copy it.
lorem-ipsum-generator.example: Asking for three sentences produces three sentences, so the output contains exactly three full stops and ends with one. Asking for five words produces exactly five words, with no full stop unless the five words happen to form a complete sentence. Asking for two paragraphs produces two blocks separated by a blank line, each with three to five sentences.

faq.q: Is this real Latin?
faq.a: No, it is a scrambled placeholder based on a passage from Cicero. It has no reliable meaning, which is the point: readers notice the layout instead of reading the words.

faq.q: Why is the text different each time?
faq.a: Words are picked in random order from the built-in list, so two presses give different results. Only the opening phrase is fixed when you turn that switch on.

faq.q: Can I choose the amount exactly?
faq.a: Yes for sentences and words. Paragraphs vary in length by design, three to five sentences each, so a paragraph count gives you that many blocks rather than an exact sentence total.

faq.q: Is the generated text saved?
faq.a: No. It is held in the page and copy is the only way out. There is no storage, account or network request.

faq.q: Why is there a maximum?
faq.a: The caps keep the tab quick and the output readable. Requests above 10 paragraphs, 30 sentences or 200 words are refused with the allowed range in the message.

text-diff-checker.title: Text diff checker
text-diff-checker.desc: Compare two versions of a text line by line. The checker marks added, removed and unchanged lines, runs entirely in your browser and never uploads a word.
text-diff-checker.lede: Paste two versions of a text and see exactly which lines were added, removed or kept. The comparison happens in your browser.
text-diff-checker.how: The tool splits both texts into lines, then builds a longest common subsequence table over the two line arrays. The table finds the largest set of lines that appear in both versions in the same order; everything outside that set is a change. Each line of the result carries a prefix: a space for an unchanged line, a minus for a line only the first version has, and a plus for a line only the second version has. Counts for added, removed and unchanged lines appear with the result, so a large change is obvious at a glance. Both inputs are capped at 40,000 characters and 1,000 lines so a huge paste cannot lock the tab, and the result is rendered as plain text rather than HTML so nothing in your text can become markup.
text-diff-checker.example: Compare a first version with the lines alpha, beta and gamma against a second version with alpha, beta two, gamma and delta. The checker keeps alpha and gamma as unchanged, reports beta as removed, and reports beta two and delta as added: one removed, two added, two unchanged. Comparing a text with itself reports zero changes and says the two versions are identical.

faq.q: Does it compare words inside a line?
faq.a: No. The comparison is line by line: any change to a line makes the whole line count as one removal and one addition. If you need finer detail, break long lines first.

faq.q: Is my text uploaded?
faq.a: No. Both texts stay in the page and the diff runs in your browser with no network request. Nothing is stored between visits.

faq.q: Why is there a size limit?
faq.a: The comparison table grows with both inputs, so each side is capped at 40,000 characters and 1,000 lines. Larger input is refused with a message rather than freezing the page.

faq.q: What do the prefixes mean?
faq.a: A leading space means the line appears in both versions, a minus means it appears only in the first version, and a plus means it appears only in the second.

faq.q: Can I copy the result?
faq.a: Yes. The difference is shown in a read-only text box with a copy button, so the prefixes and line breaks copy with it.

roman-numerals.title: Roman numeral converter
roman-numerals.desc: Convert any number from 1 to 3999 into a Roman numeral and back again, with the working shown step by step. Free and private in your browser.
roman-numerals.lede: Type a number from 1 to 3999 to get its Roman numeral, or switch direction and type a numeral to get the number. The working is shown alongside the answer.
roman-numerals.how: Roman numerals are written with seven letters: I, V, X, L, C, D and M for 1, 5, 10, 50, 100, 500 and 1000. A smaller letter before a larger one subtracts it, so IV is 4 and XC is 90; otherwise the values add, so VI is 6. To convert a number, the tool walks down the value table, taking as many of each step as fit: 1994 takes M (1000), then CM (900), then XC (90), then IV (4). In the other direction it reads each letter, subtracting when the next letter is larger and adding otherwise, and checks the result against the canonical pattern so strict forms such as IIII or IC are refused. Only whole numbers from 1 to 3999 are accepted.
roman-numerals.example: 1994 becomes MCMXCIV: M covers 1000, CM covers 900, XC covers 90 and IV covers 4, and 1000 + 900 + 90 + 4 = 1994. Reading MCMXCIV back gives the same 1994, because each subtractive pair is in its canonical place.

faq.q: Why does it stop at 3999?
faq.a: Standard Roman notation has no clean way to write 4000 without a bar over the letters, which this tool does not render. Anything outside 1 to 3999 is refused with a message instead of guessing.

faq.q: Why is IIII rejected?
faq.a: Clock faces often show IIII for four, but the canonical form is IV. The tool accepts the canonical form only, so the same numeral always converts to the same number.

faq.q: Can it convert lowercase letters?
faq.a: Yes. Lowercase input is read the same way as uppercase, so typing cmxciv gives the same answer as CMXCIV.

faq.q: Is this a valid way to write dates?
faq.a: It is the classical form, but styles vary by period and publisher. For example, 2024 is MMXXIV here, while some inscriptions would write it differently.

faq.q: Is my input stored?
faq.a: No. Conversion happens in this tab with no storage and no network request. Reload the page and the field is empty.

number-base-converter.title: Number base converter
number-base-converter.desc: Convert a number between binary, octal, decimal, hexadecimal and any base from 2 to 36, with big values kept exact. Free and private online.
number-base-converter.lede: Enter a value in one base and read it in binary, octal, decimal, hexadecimal, base 36 and a custom base of your choice. Large values stay exact.
number-base-converter.how: A base is the number of digits available. Decimal uses 0 to 9, binary uses 0 and 1, hexadecimal adds A to F, and a custom base up to 36 continues through Z. To read a value, the tool multiplies each digit's place from the right: the rightmost digit is worth base to the power 0, the next base to the power 1, and so on. To write it in another base it repeatedly divides and keeps the remainder, which becomes the next digit — 1000 divided by 2 is 500 remainder 0, and so on up to 1111101000. Every digit is parsed into a BigInt, so values far beyond the safe integer range convert without losing precision. Digits that do not belong to the chosen base are rejected with the offending character named.
number-base-converter.example: The value 1000 in decimal converts to 1111101000 in binary, 1750 in octal, 3E8 in hexadecimal and RS in base 36. Each of those reads back to exactly 1000, which is why the decimal row always repeats your input unchanged.

faq.q: What does a custom base mean?
faq.a: Any base from 2 to 36. Digits run 0 to 9 then A to Z, so base 36 uses every character a single digit can hold. The tool validates each digit against the chosen base.

faq.q: How large can the value be?
faq.a: The input is limited to 120 characters, and values are held as BigInt rather than JavaScript numbers, so a 100-digit value converts exactly with no rounding.

faq.q: Why are hexadecimal digits uppercase?
faq.a: Both cases are accepted on input, and output is shown uppercase because that is the common convention in code, checksums and colour values.

faq.q: Can I enter fractions or minus values?
faq.a: No. This is an integer converter: fractions and negative signs are refused with their own message so the answer is never a silently rounded value.

faq.q: Is the conversion private?
faq.a: Yes. Parsing and formatting happen in this tab. There is no request, storage or history — the value disappears when you reload.

color-contrast-checker.title: Colour contrast checker
color-contrast-checker.desc: Check the WCAG 2 contrast ratio between two colours and see the AA and AAA results for normal and large text. Free, instant and private.
color-contrast-checker.lede: Enter a text colour and a background colour as hex values to get the exact WCAG 2 contrast ratio and pass or fail results for AA and AAA text.
color-contrast-checker.how: WCAG defines contrast from relative luminance. Each channel of a hex colour is converted from sRGB to a linear value, where a channel c is c/12.92 below 0.03928 and ((c + 0.055) / 1.055)^2.4 above it. The luminance of the colour is 0.2126 times red, plus 0.7152 times green, plus 0.0722 times blue. The ratio is then (lighter + 0.05) divided by (darker + 0.05), which ranges from 1:1 for identical colours to 21:1 for black on white. AA needs 4.5 for normal text and 3 for large text; AAA needs 7 and 4.5. Large text means at least 24 pixels, or 18.66 pixels when bold. Enter hex as #rgb or #rrggbb, with or without the hash.
color-contrast-checker.example: Grey #777777 on white #ffffff gives luminance 0.1845 for the grey and 1.0000 for white, so the ratio is (1.0000 + 0.05) divided by (0.1845 + 0.05) = 4.48 to 1. That passes AA for large text at 3:1 but misses the 4.5 requirement for normal text — which is why #777 body copy on white fails an audit.

faq.q: What does the ratio mean?
faq.a: It is the difference in perceived brightness between the two colours, from 1:1 (identical) to 21:1 (black on white). WCAG sets minimum ratios so text stays readable.

faq.q: Which number do I need to pass?
faq.a: 4.5:1 for normal text under AA, 3:1 for large text under AA, 7:1 for normal text under AAA and 4.5:1 for large text under AAA. The four rows report each one separately.

faq.q: Why does #777 on white fail?
faq.a: Its ratio is 4.48:1, just under the 4.5:1 needed for normal text. Slightly darker grey such as #767676 crosses the threshold and passes.

faq.q: Does it handle three-digit hex?
faq.a: Yes. #abc is read as #aabbcc, the usual shorthand. Any other format is refused with a message naming the format expected.

faq.q: Does this check my whole page?
faq.a: No, it compares two colours. Use it for text against its background, then repeat for the other pairs such as link text, buttons and placeholder text.

average-calculator.title: Average calculator
average-calculator.desc: Paste any list of numbers to get the mean, median, mode, range, count and sum, with invalid entries ignored and reported. Free and private.
average-calculator.lede: Paste numbers separated by commas, spaces or line breaks to get the mean, median, mode, range, count and sum in one step. Tokens that are not numbers are listed so none are missed.
average-calculator.how: Enter the numbers in any list form: commas, spaces, semicolons or new lines all separate values. The count is how many numbers were read and the sum adds them all. The mean divides the sum by the count. For the median the list is sorted first, then the middle value is taken, or the average of the two middle values when the count is even. The mode is the value that appears most often, shown as a list when several tie; if nothing repeats, the tool says so instead of inventing one. The range is the largest value minus the smallest. Tokens that are not plain numbers are ignored and listed below the result so you can see exactly what was left out.
average-calculator.example: For 4, 8, 15, 16, 23 and 42 the count is 6, the sum is 108 and the mean is 108 divided by 6, which is 18. Sorted, the list puts 15 and 16 in the middle, so the median is (15 + 16) divided by 2, which is 15.5. No value repeats, so there is no mode, and the range is 42 minus 4, which is 38.

faq.q: How do I enter the numbers?
faq.a: Any way you like: 1, 2, 3 or 1 2 3 or each on its own line. Semicolons work too. Anything that is not a plain number is skipped and listed under the result.

faq.q: What is the difference between mean and median?
faq.a: The mean is the sum divided by the count, so one very large value pulls it up. The median is the middle value after sorting, so outliers barely move it.

faq.q: Why does it say there is no mode?
faq.a: A mode only exists when a value repeats. When every number appears once, reporting a mode would be misleading, so the tool states that instead.

faq.q: Does it ignore negative numbers?
faq.a: No. Minus values are normal numbers and are included in every statistic. Only tokens that are not numbers at all are excluded, and they are shown in the message.

faq.q: How many numbers can I paste?
faq.a: Up to 10,000 values in 20,000 characters. Beyond either cap the tool refuses with the limit in the message rather than slowing the page down.

slug-generator.title: Slug generator
slug-generator.desc: Turn any heading into a clean URL slug: lowercased, accents removed, symbols stripped and the separator you choose. Runs in your browser and nothing is saved.
slug-generator.lede: Paste a title or any text and get a URL-safe slug back: lowercased, accents stripped, symbols removed, with the separator you pick.
slug-generator.how: The text is lowercased first, then Unicode-normalised so accented letters lose their marks: Café becomes cafe and Zürich becomes Zurich, while ß is expanded to ss. Every run of characters that is not a letter or a digit collapses into one separator. Separators are trimmed from both ends, so a title that starts with punctuation still yields a clean slug. The input is capped at 500 characters and anything longer is refused with a clear message rather than silently cut. The result appears as plain text with a copy button, and the conversion runs entirely in this page.
slug-generator.example: Take the heading "Café Zürich 2026!" with the hyphen separator. Lowercasing gives café zürich 2026!, dropping the accent marks gives cafe zurich 2026, and replacing the space and the exclamation mark with the separator gives cafe-zurich-2026. Switching the separator to an underscore produces cafe_zurich_2026 from the same text. A title made only of symbols such as "###" has nothing to keep, so the tool says so instead of showing an empty or broken slug.

faq.q: Why are accents removed?
faq.a: URL slugs are usually plain ASCII so they survive copying, sharing and older software. Dropping the marks turns Café into cafe while the word stays readable.

faq.q: Can I choose the separator?
faq.a: Yes. Hyphen, underscore and space are offered, and the hyphen is the default because it is the usual choice in URLs.

faq.q: What happens to long text?
faq.a: The input is capped at 500 characters. Longer text is refused with a message, so the page stays fast and the slug stays short.

faq.q: Does it check whether the slug already exists?
faq.a: No. It converts one piece of text. Checking a database for duplicates is something your site or CMS does when it saves the record.

faq.q: Is my text stored or sent anywhere?
faq.a: No. The conversion runs in the browser. Nothing is written to storage and nothing is sent over the network.

html-entity-encoder.title: HTML entity encoder
html-entity-encoder.desc: Encode text into HTML entities or decode entities back to plain text. The output stays text, never markup, and everything runs in your browser.
html-entity-encoder.lede: Encode special characters as HTML entities, or paste entities and decode them back to readable text. The result is shown as plain text only.
html-entity-encoder.how: Encoding handles the five characters that matter in markup, always in the safe order: the ampersand becomes & first, so no entity this tool creates is decoded again by mistake, then < becomes <, > becomes >, the double quote becomes " and the apostrophe becomes '. Decoding runs a single pass over the common named entities (&, <, >, " and  ) and over decimal and hexadecimal numeric forms, so a sequence such as &lt; decodes exactly one level. Input is capped at 20,000 characters, and the result is written into a read-only text box rather than into the page as markup.
html-entity-encoder.example: Encoding the fragment Tom & Jerry's gives <b>Tom & Jerry's</b>. Decoding that output returns the original Tom & Jerry's character for character. Encoding a plain string such as hello world returns it unchanged, and an unknown entity such as &foo; is left exactly as typed instead of being silently dropped.

faq.q: Which characters are encoded?
faq.a: Five: the ampersand, the less-than and greater-than signs, the double quote and the apostrophe. The ampersand is always replaced first so the output cannot mislead a parser.

faq.q: Why is the result plain text?
faq.a: The result sits in a text box, so a fragment you encode can be copied without the browser rendering it as markup. User input is never inserted into the page as HTML.

faq.q: Does it decode every named entity?
faq.a: It handles the ones that appear on real pages — &, <, >, " and   — plus decimal and hexadecimal numeric references. Unknown names are left untouched.

faq.q: Is there a size limit?
faq.a: Yes, 20,000 characters. Longer input is refused with a clear message rather than partially converted.

faq.q: Is anything uploaded?
faq.a: No. Encoding and decoding are string operations that run in your browser; no request carries your text anywhere.

jwt-decoder.title: JWT decoder
jwt-decoder.desc: Decode a JWT header and payload in your browser. The token is never sent, never verified, and a decoded token proves nothing about its validity.
jwt-decoder.lede: Paste a JSON Web Token to see its header and payload as readable JSON. Nothing is verified and the token never leaves this page.
jwt-decoder.how: A JWT is three base64url segments separated by dots: header, payload and signature. The tool splits on the dots, restores the base64url alphabet (dashes back to plus, underscores to slash, padding added) and decodes each segment as UTF-8 JSON. Header and payload are pretty-printed; the signature is shown but never checked, because verifying it needs the secret or public key only the issuer holds. Numeric time claims — iat, exp and nbf — are also listed as UTC dates next to their raw epoch seconds. A segment longer than 6,000 characters, a token that is not two or three parts, or a segment that fails to parse each get a specific message.
jwt-decoder.example: The public sample token eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiIxMjM0NTY3ODkwIiwibmFtZSI6IkpvaG4gRG9lIiwiaWF0IjoxNTE2MjM5MDIyfQ.SflKxwRJSMeKKF2QT4fwpMeJf36POk6yJV_adQssw5c decodes to a header of alg HS256 with typ JWT, and a payload of sub 1234567890, name John Doe and iat 1516239022, which the tool shows as Thu, 18 Jan 2018 01:30:22 GMT. The third segment is displayed as-is and never verified, and the page states that a decoded token is not proof that it is valid.

faq.q: Does this verify the signature?
faq.a: No. Verification requires the secret or the public key that the issuer used. This tool only decodes, so it never confirms that the token is genuine or untampered.

faq.q: Is my token sent anywhere?
faq.a: No. Decoding is string work done in the page. The token is not stored, logged or transmitted.

faq.q: Why do you say a decoded token is not proof?
faq.a: Anyone can edit a payload and re-encode it without a valid signature. Only a server that verifies the signature can trust what the claims say.

faq.q: What happens with a malformed token?
faq.a: A token that is not two or three dot-separated parts, a segment that is not valid base64url, or JSON that does not parse each produce their own clear message rather than a blank panel.

faq.q: Why are the dates shown twice?
faq.a: iat, exp and nbf hold epoch seconds. The tool shows the raw number and the UTC date so you can read both without converting anything by hand.

csv-json-converter.title: CSV to JSON converter
csv-json-converter.desc: Convert CSV to JSON or JSON to CSV in your browser, with quoted fields, embedded commas and line breaks inside quotes handled correctly. Nothing is uploaded.
csv-json-converter.lede: Paste CSV to get JSON, or paste JSON to get CSV. Quoted fields, embedded commas, embedded line breaks and an optional header row are all handled.
csv-json-converter.how: The CSV parser reads character by character: inside double quotes a comma or a newline belongs to the field, and two quotes in a row mean one literal quote. With the header row ticked, the first line supplies the keys and every later line supplies values; short rows are filled with empty strings and a row with more fields than the header is reported by number. Turning JSON back into CSV takes the keys of the first object as the header and quotes any value containing a comma, a quote or a newline, doubling the quotes inside it. Input is capped at 200,000 characters and 2,000 rows, and both directions run locally.
csv-json-converter.example: The three lines name,qty,price then Widget,3,2.50 then "Bolt, long",7,0.10 become a JSON array of two objects: name Widget with qty 3 and price 2.50, and name Bolt, long with qty 7 and price 0.10 — the comma inside the quotes stays in the name field. Values stay strings, so 2.50 keeps its trailing zero. Converting that JSON back with the header row ticked reproduces the original three lines exactly.

faq.q: Are numbers turned into JSON numbers?
faq.a: No. Every value stays a string, so an identifier like 007 or a price like 2.50 survives the round trip exactly as you typed it.

faq.q: How are quotes inside a field handled?
faq.a: Two quotes in a row read as one literal quote, and when writing CSV, any value with a comma, quote or newline is wrapped in quotes with its inner quotes doubled.

faq.q: What if rows have different lengths?
faq.a: Rows with fewer fields than the header are filled with empty strings. A row with extra fields is reported with its row number and the extra values are dropped.

faq.q: What forms of JSON are accepted?
faq.a: An array of objects, an array of arrays, or a single object, which is treated as one row. Anything else gets an invalid JSON message.

faq.q: Is there a size limit?
faq.a: Yes: 200,000 characters and 2,000 rows. Larger input is refused with a clear message so the page stays responsive.

sort-lines.title: Sort lines
sort-lines.desc: Sort lines of text A to Z, Z to A, numerically or by length, with an option to remove empty lines. Everything runs in your browser and input is capped.
sort-lines.lede: Paste a list and sort it A to Z, Z to A, by number or by line length, with an option to drop empty lines. The result is a text block you can copy.
sort-lines.how: The text is split on line breaks, and one trailing line break counts as an ending rather than a blank line. A to Z compares whole lines character by character, so digits sort before capitals because the code for 1 is lower than the code for A, and Z to A reverses that order. Numeric sorting parses each line as a number and pushes lines that are not numbers to the end in their original order, with a warning that counts them. Sorting by length compares character counts and keeps the original order between equal lengths. The remove-empty option drops blank lines before any sort. Input is capped at 50,000 characters and 5,000 lines.
sort-lines.example: The four lines pear, Apple, 10 and banana sort to 10, Apple, banana, pear from A to Z, because digits are coded lower than capitals, and to pear, banana, Apple, 10 from Z to A. By length they become 10, pear, Apple, banana, since 10 has 2 characters, pear has 4, Apple has 5 and banana has 6. A numeric sort of 10, -2 and 3.5 gives -2, 3.5, 10, and any word left in that list is named in a warning instead of being sorted by mistake.

faq.q: Why do numbers sort before letters?
faq.a: A to Z compares character codes, and the digit 1 is coded lower than the capital A, so 10 comes first. Use the numeric order when the lines are numbers.

faq.q: What happens to blank lines?
faq.a: They keep their place by default. Tick remove empty lines and they are dropped before the sort runs.

faq.q: What about non-numeric lines in a numeric sort?
faq.a: They are placed at the end in the order you typed them, and a warning tells you how many there were.

faq.q: Is there a size limit?
faq.a: Yes: 50,000 characters and 5,000 lines. Larger input is refused with a clear message rather than freezing the page.

faq.q: Is my list stored?
faq.a: No. Sorting happens in the browser, nothing is written to storage and nothing is sent over the network.

working-days-calculator.title: Working days calculator
working-days-calculator.desc: Count working days between two dates with your own holiday list and your own weekend days. Runs in your browser and stores nothing.
working-days-calculator.lede: Pick two dates, tick the days that make up your weekend and list your holidays. The tool counts the working days, the weekend days and the holidays in between.
working-days-calculator.how: The tool reads both dates as plain calendar dates, then walks every day from the start up to and including the end. Each day is checked in order: if its weekday is ticked as a weekend day it is counted as weekend, if its date appears in your holiday list it is counted as a holiday, and otherwise it counts as a working day. The three counts always add up to the calendar days in the range, so the arithmetic is visible. Weekend days default to Saturday and Sunday but any of the seven weekdays can be ticked. Holidays are one yyyy-mm-dd date per line, and an empty list is fine.
working-days-calculator.example: From Monday 2 March 2026 to Friday 13 March 2026, with Saturday and Sunday as the weekend and no holidays, the tool counts 10 working days and 2 weekend days across 12 calendar days: the first week contributes Monday to Friday, the weekend takes two days, and the second week contributes Monday to Friday again. Adding Tuesday 10 March 2026 to the holiday list drops the working total to 9 while the calendar total stays at 12.

faq.q: Are the dates local or UTC?
faq.a: They are the calendar dates you typed, compared by year, month and day, so no time zone can push a day across the boundary.

faq.q: Can I choose which days count as the weekend?
faq.a: Yes. All seven weekdays are tickable, so a Saturday-Sunday weekend, a Friday-Sunday weekend or a six-day week all work.

faq.q: How do I add holidays?

faq.q: What if the end date is before the start date?

faq.q: Is my holiday list stored?

fraction-calculator.title: Fraction calculator
fraction-calculator.desc: Work with fractions step by step: add, subtract, multiply and divide, then see the fraction in lowest terms, the mixed number and the decimal.
fraction-calculator.lede: Enter two fractions and pick an operation. The answer comes back as a fraction in lowest terms, a mixed number and a decimal.
fraction-calculator.how: Addition and subtraction find the lowest common denominator, rewrite both fractions over it and add the numerators. Multiplication multiplies the two numerators and the two denominators directly. Division flips the second fraction and multiplies. The result is then reduced by dividing top and bottom by their greatest common divisor, which also turns a negative denominator positive by moving the sign to the numerator. An improper result is shown as a mixed number as well, and the decimal is the numerator divided by the denominator. Denominators must be whole numbers other than zero.
fraction-calculator.example: Take 6/8 + 3/4. Over the common denominator 8 that is 6/8 + 6/8 = 12/8, which divides by 4 to give 3/2 in lowest terms. As a mixed number that is 1 1/2, and 3 divided by 2 is 1.5. A zero denominator is refused instead of producing an error, because dividing by zero has no answer.

faq.q: Why must the denominators be whole numbers?
faq.a: A fraction is a ratio of two integers. Enter 3 for three halves rather than 1.5, and the working stays exact instead of drifting into rounding.

faq.q: How is the fraction reduced?
faq.a: The numerator and denominator are divided by their greatest common divisor, so 12/8 becomes 3/2 with no approximation involved.

faq.q: What does the mixed number mean?
faq.a: It splits an improper fraction into whole parts and a remainder: 3/2 is one whole and one half, written 1 1/2. Proper fractions show the same value as the reduced fraction.

faq.q: What happens with a zero denominator?
faq.a: The calculation is refused with a clear message. Dividing by zero has no result, so no number is invented.

faq.q: Is anything stored or sent?
faq.a: No. The arithmetic runs in this page with plain numbers; nothing is written to storage or sent over the network.

ratio-calculator.title: Ratio calculator
ratio-calculator.desc: Simplify a ratio, scale it by a factor or solve a missing value in a proportion, with every step shown. Runs in your browser, nothing is stored.
ratio-calculator.lede: Three jobs in one tool: reduce a ratio to its simplest form, scale it by a factor, or solve for the missing value in a proportion.
ratio-calculator.how: Simplifying divides both sides by their greatest common divisor until they share no common factor, so 42:58 becomes 21:29. Scaling multiplies both sides by the factor and leaves the ratio in the same relationship, so 3:5 times 4 is 12:20. Solving a proportion uses the cross product: from a:b as c:x the missing value is x = b times c divided by a. Zero is refused in any position because a ratio with a zero side carries no relationship, and a zero scale factor would collapse the ratio to 0:0.
ratio-calculator.example: The ratio 42:58 simplifies to 21:29 because both sides divide by 2. Scaling 3:5 by a factor of 4 gives 12:20, which still simplifies back to 3:5. Solving 3:5 = 18:x uses x = 5 times 18 divided by 3, so the missing value is 30 and the finished proportion reads 3:5 = 18:30.

faq.q: Which form of the ratio is shown?
faq.a: The simplest form using whole numbers, plus the total number of parts, which is useful when splitting something between sides.

faq.q: Why is zero refused?
faq.a: A side of zero means the two quantities are not in proportion, and a scale factor of zero would produce 0:0, which tells you nothing.

faq.q: How is the missing value calculated?
faq.a: By the cross product: in a:b as c:x, x equals b times c divided by a. The finished proportion is printed next to the answer so you can check it.

faq.q: Can I use decimals?
faq.a: Yes. Decimals and negatives are accepted for the values and the scale factor; only zero is rejected.

faq.q: Is my calculation stored?
faq.a: No. The numbers stay in the page while you use the tool, and nothing is saved or transmitted.

stopwatch-timer.title: Stopwatch and timer
stopwatch-timer.desc: A stopwatch with start, pause, reset and laps, measured with performance.now() in this tab. No storage, no cookies, nothing sent anywhere.
stopwatch-timer.lede: Start, pause, reset and record laps. The time is measured with performance.now() in this tab and never written anywhere.
stopwatch-timer.how: The display reads the clock with performance.now(), which counts in milliseconds from a fixed point and is not affected by the wall clock changing. While running, the reading is the accumulated time from earlier runs plus the time since the current start, so pausing and resuming never loses or double-counts a millisecond. The display refreshes on a short interval that recomputes the total instead of adding ticks, so a throttled or hidden tab still shows the right time when you come back. A lap stores the reading at the moment you press it.
stopwatch-timer.example: Start the stopwatch, wait about a second and press Lap: the first lap shows the elapsed time at that moment. Press Lap again after another two seconds and the second lap reads about three seconds in total, because laps record the total running time, not the gap. Pause and the reading freezes exactly where it is; reset returns everything to 00:00.00 and clears the laps.

faq.q: What happens when the tab is in the background?
faq.a: The reading is always recomputed from performance.now(), so browser throttling cannot make the stopwatch drift. The value you see after switching back is correct.

faq.q: Are laps kept when I close the page?
faq.a: No. Nothing is stored in cookies or storage, so laps and the current time live only in the page while it is open.

faq.q: How precise is the display?
faq.a: It shows tenths of a second, while the underlying measurement is in milliseconds. It is a stopwatch for everyday timing, not an instrument.

faq.q: Can I pause and continue?
faq.a: Yes. Pause freezes the reading, and starting again continues from that point rather than from zero.

faq.q: Is any data sent anywhere?
faq.a: No. The stopwatch makes no requests and stores nothing; it is pure timing code in this page.

image-to-base64.title: Image to Base64 encoder
image-to-base64.desc: Turn an image into a Base64 data URI in your browser. The file is never uploaded, the size limit is stated, and the result comes with a copy button.
image-to-base64.lede: Choose an image and get a data URI back, with the file name, size and type shown alongside a copy button. The file never leaves this page.
image-to-base64.how: The file is read with the FileReader API as a data URL, which is the raw bytes of the image encoded in Base64 behind a prefix such as data:image/png;base64,. A progress bar shows the read while it happens, so a larger file does not look like a stalled page. Only files whose type starts with image are accepted, and anything over 5 MB is refused with a message that states the limit. The result is written into a read-only text box you can copy straight into an HTML file or a stylesheet.
image-to-base64.example: A 1 KB PNG of 1,024 bytes becomes a data URI of about 1,372 characters, because Base64 turns every three bytes into four characters and adds a short prefix. Choosing a text file such as notes.txt does not produce an encoding at all: the tool says the file is not an image and stops before reading it, and a file over 5 MB is refused with the limit in the message.

faq.q: Is my image uploaded?
faq.a: No. The file is read by the browser itself with FileReader and never sent anywhere. Nothing is stored between visits.

faq.q: What is the size limit?
faq.a: 5 MB. Larger files are refused with a message stating the limit, so the page never freezes while encoding something huge.

faq.q: Which file types are accepted?
faq.a: Anything the browser reports as an image: PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, SVG and the rest. Other files are refused before they are read.

faq.q: Why is the data URI longer than the file?
faq.a: Base64 encodes three bytes as four characters, so the text grows by about a third plus the short data prefix. That is the format, not an overhead added by the tool.

faq.q: Can I use the result directly?
faq.a: Yes. Paste the data URI into a src attribute, a CSS url() or a fetch body. For anything larger than a few hundred kilobytes a real file is usually the better choice.

salary-to-hourly.title: Salary to hourly calculator
salary-to-hourly.desc: Turn a yearly salary into an hourly, daily, weekly and monthly figure using the hours you actually work. Arithmetic only, no tax rules.
salary-to-hourly.lede: Enter a yearly salary plus the hours and weeks you work, and the tool divides it down to an hourly rate with the daily, weekly and monthly equivalents.
salary-to-hourly.how: The hourly rate is the yearly salary divided by the paid hours in a year, and those hours are your hours per week multiplied by your weeks per year. Forty hours over fifty-two weeks is 2,080 hours, so a 52,000 salary gives 25.00 an hour. The weekly figure divides the salary by the number of weeks, the monthly figure divides it by twelve, and the daily figure takes the hourly rate and multiplies it by the weekly hours divided by five. Every result is printed with the arithmetic that produced it, so you can check each line yourself. No tax, pension or holiday rules are applied: the tool only divides the number you type.
salary-to-hourly.example: For a 52,000 salary at 40 hours a week over 52 weeks, the paid hours are 40 × 52 = 2,080. The hourly rate is 52,000 ÷ 2,080 = 25.00. The daily figure is 25.00 × (40 ÷ 5) = 200.00, the weekly figure is 52,000 ÷ 52 = 1,000.00, and the monthly figure is 52,000 ÷ 12 = 4,333.33.

faq.q: Does this include tax?
faq.a: No. It is arithmetic only: no income tax, national insurance, pension or student loan is subtracted. Type the gross salary to compare job offers, or a net figure if you already know your take-home pay.

faq.q: Why divide by hours per week times weeks per year?
faq.a: Because that product is the number of paid hours in a year. At 40 hours over 52 weeks it is 2,080 hours, so dividing the salary by 2,080 gives the rate for each paid hour.

faq.q: Should I use 52 weeks if I get paid holiday?
faq.a: Use the number of weeks you are actually paid for. If your salary is spread across the full year including holiday, keep 52. If you are paid only for weeks worked, enter the smaller number.

faq.q: How is the daily figure worked out?
faq.a: The hourly rate is multiplied by your weekly hours divided by five. That assumes five working days sharing the same weekly hours, so it is an average, not a timesheet.

faq.q: What if my hours change from week to week?
faq.a: Enter an average week. The result is a straight division, so it can only be as accurate as that average.

keyword-density-analyzer.title: Keyword density analyzer
keyword-density-analyzer.desc: Paste text to see how often each word appears, with counts and percentages from a stated formula. Up to 50,000 characters, nothing uploaded.
keyword-density-analyzer.lede: Paste an article or a page of copy to see which words repeat and what share of the text each one takes, with the formula printed beside the result.
keyword-density-analyzer.how: The text is split into words: runs of letters and digits, keeping apostrophes and hyphens that sit inside a word, so "don't" counts once. Every word is lowercased, then counted. Density for a word is its count divided by the total number of words, multiplied by one hundred, and that number is what the percentage column shows. Ties are listed alphabetically. Ticking the option to ignore common words removes a built-in list of function words such as "the" and "and" from both the count and the total, so the percentages then describe only the remaining words. The input is capped at 50,000 characters and 20,000 words, and the twelve most frequent words are shown.
keyword-density-analyzer.example: For "The cat sat on the mat. The cat slept." the tool reads nine words: the, cat, sat, on, the, mat, the, cat and slept. "the" appears three times, so its density is 3 ÷ 9 × 100 = 33.33%. "cat" appears twice, so 2 ÷ 9 × 100 = 22.22%. The four remaining words appear once each, which is 11.11% each, and there are six different words in total.

faq.q: What counts as a word here?
faq.a: A run of letters and digits. Apostrophes and hyphens are kept when they sit between characters, so "don't" and "e-mail" each count once. Punctuation on its own is ignored.

faq.q: Why do the percentages change when I ignore common words?
faq.a: The option removes the stop words from both the count and the total, so the percentages are recalculated over the remaining words. They will not add up to the same totals as the full text.

faq.q: Does keyword density affect search rankings?
faq.a: I cannot tell you a ranking effect from this tool, and it makes no such claim. It reports how often words repeat in the text you paste, which is all the numbers measure.

faq.q: Is my text uploaded anywhere?
faq.a: No. The counting runs in the page with JavaScript. Nothing is sent, stored or written to a cookie.

faq.q: How many words are listed?
faq.a: The twelve most frequent, highest first, with ties in alphabetical order. The totals above the list cover the whole input, not just those twelve.

meta-tag-generator.title: Meta tag generator
meta-tag-generator.desc: Build a title, description, canonical, Open Graph and Twitter card block as plain text, with length counters as you type. Nothing is uploaded.
meta-tag-generator.lede: Fill in the page details and copy a ready block of head tags, with a live character count for the title and the description.
meta-tag-generator.how: The tool assembles the tags in a fixed order: the title element, the description, the canonical link, the Open Graph tags, then the Twitter card tags. Open Graph and Twitter tags repeat the title, description and image under different attribute names because each service reads a different set. Attribute values are escaped, so an ampersand becomes & and a double quote becomes ", which keeps the block valid HTML. The two counters show the title and description lengths against 60 and 160 characters, the usual display lengths in search results; going over them is allowed but may be truncated. Optional fields are skipped when left empty, so a page with no image simply gets no image tags. Everything is produced in the browser as text.
meta-tag-generator.example: With the title "Blue mug — Stacklane" (20 characters), the description "A 350 ml ceramic mug." (21 characters), the URL https://YOURDOMAIN.com/mug.html, the image https://YOURDOMAIN.com/mug.png and the site name Stacklane, the tool prints thirteen lines. The first three are <title>Blue mug — Stacklane</title>, then <meta name="description" content="A 350 ml ceramic mug.">, then <link rel="canonical" href="https://YOURDOMAIN.com/mug.html">. The block ends with the Twitter card and image tags for the same page.

faq.q: Where do these tags go?
faq.a: Inside the head element of the page, before the closing </head>. Paste the whole block as it is; the order inside head does not matter to browsers.

faq.q: Will this improve my ranking?
faq.a: No claim is made about rankings. A title and description are what a search engine may show for the page, and whether it uses them is its decision, not something this tool can guarantee.

faq.q: Why is twitter:card always summary_large_image?
faq.a: Because it tells the service to use a wide image. If your image is small or square, change that value to "summary" by hand after pasting.

faq.q: Are the 60 and 160 counters hard limits?
faq.a: They are the lengths usually shown in results before truncation, not limits on what HTML accepts. Text over them is valid; it may simply be cut off in a preview.

faq.q: Does the generator escape special characters?
faq.a: Yes. Ampersands, angle brackets and double quotes in your text are written as entities, so a title containing an ampersand still produces valid HTML.

robots-txt-generator.title: Robots.txt generator
robots-txt-generator.desc: Write a robots.txt in plain text: allow everything, block everything or list your own paths, then add a sitemap line. Free, in your browser.
robots-txt-generator.lede: Choose what crawlers may fetch, list any paths of your own, and copy a finished robots.txt with each directive explained.
robots-txt-generator.how: The file is built from directives, one per line. User-agent names the crawler the following rules apply to, and an asterisk means all of them. Disallow lists paths that must not be fetched, and an empty Disallow means nothing is blocked, which is how a file allows everything. A line starting with a bang in the paths box becomes an Allow line instead, so you can block a folder and reopen one file inside it. Blank lines separate groups and are ignored. The optional Sitemap line takes a full URL and points crawlers at the sitemap; it is not part of any group. Paths must start with a slash. The output is plain text you can copy or download as robots.txt.
robots-txt-generator.example: With "allow everything" selected and the sitemap https://YOURDOMAIN.com/sitemap.xml, the tool writes three lines: User-agent: * then Disallow: with nothing after it, then a blank line and Sitemap: https://YOURDOMAIN.com/sitemap.xml. The empty Disallow is deliberate: it means no path is blocked, which is the usual way to say everything is allowed.

faq.q: Does robots.txt remove a page from search results?
faq.a: Not reliably. It asks crawlers not to fetch a URL, but a blocked page can still appear in results if other sites link to it. To keep a page out of results, let it be crawled and send a noindex robots meta tag instead.

faq.q: Where does robots.txt have to live?
faq.a: At the root of the domain, so the address is https://YOURDOMAIN.com/robots.txt. A copy in a subfolder is not read for that domain.

faq.q: What does an empty Disallow line mean?
faq.a: Nothing is disallowed, so every path may be fetched. That is the standard way to allow a whole site while still naming the user agent.

faq.q: Can I block a folder but allow one file inside it?
faq.a: Yes, in custom mode. Add a line for the folder and prefix the file's line with an exclamation mark to make it an Allow rule; most crawlers then use the longest matching rule.

faq.q: Do all crawlers follow these rules?
faq.a: Most well-known search crawlers do. Any crawler is free to ignore the file, so it is a request rather than a lock.

xml-sitemap-generator.title: XML sitemap generator
xml-sitemap-generator.desc: Paste page URLs to get a valid sitemap.xml: escaped characters, duplicates removed, and your chosen change frequency and priority.
xml-sitemap-generator.lede: Paste one URL per line and the tool writes a complete sitemap XML file, escaping special characters and dropping duplicates on the way.
xml-sitemap-generator.how: Each non-empty line is checked as a URL that starts with http or https and contains a domain. Lines that fail are reported with the text that caused the problem, and duplicates are removed with a count. The surviving URLs are written as url entries inside a urlset element, each with a loc element, the change frequency you picked and the priority you picked. Five characters are escaped as XML entities: ampersands, angle brackets, double quotes and apostrophes, because an unescaped ampersand makes the file invalid. The result is capped at 5,000 URLs. You can copy it or download it as sitemap.xml. The file is assembled in the browser and nothing is uploaded.
xml-sitemap-generator.example: Pasting https://YOURDOMAIN.com/ and https://YOURDOMAIN.com/list.html?tag=a&sort=2 with monthly frequency and priority 0.7 produces a file that starts with the XML declaration and the urlset element, then two url blocks. In the second block the loc line reads https://YOURDOMAIN.com/list.html?tag=a&sort=2, because the ampersand must be escaped for the XML to be valid. The file closes with the urlset end tag.

faq.q: What is a sitemap actually for?
faq.a: It is a list of URLs you want crawlers to know about. It helps them find pages, but it does not guarantee that a page is crawled, indexed or ranked.

faq.q: Why is the ampersand replaced with &?
faq.a: XML reserves the ampersand, so a raw one makes the document invalid and a parser will reject it. Writing & is the correct way to include an ampersand in a URL inside XML.

faq.q: How many URLs can I add?
faq.a: This page accepts 5,000. The sitemap format itself allows up to 50,000 URLs and 50 MB per file, beyond which you split into several files and an index.

faq.q: Do changefreq and priority matter?
faq.a: They are hints. Major crawlers have said they ignore both, so the file is still useful without them; keep the values honest rather than optimistic.

faq.q: Where should the file go?
faq.a: At the site root as sitemap.xml, and reference it in robots.txt with a Sitemap line so crawlers can find it.

css-box-shadow-generator.title: CSS box shadow generator
css-box-shadow-generator.desc: Set offset, blur, spread, colour and opacity to build a box-shadow rule, copy the CSS and see it on a sample card. Inset is supported.
css-box-shadow-generator.lede: Adjust the offset, blur, spread, colour and opacity, watch the shadow on a sample card, then copy the finished declaration.
css-box-shadow-generator.how: A box shadow takes an optional inset keyword, then the horizontal offset, the vertical offset, the blur radius, the spread radius and a colour, all in that order. Offsets move the shadow away from the element: positive x moves it right and positive y moves it down. The blur radius softens the edge and cannot be negative, while the spread grows the shadow before it is blurred and may be negative to shrink it. The colour field takes a hex value, which is converted to rgba so the opacity field can set the alpha channel separately. The tool rejects values outside these ranges with a specific message, and shows the exact declaration it built.
css-box-shadow-generator.example: With x 2, y 4, blur 8, spread 0, the colour #000000 and opacity 0.2, the tool produces box-shadow: 2px 4px 8px 0px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.2);. That is a black shadow moved 2 pixels right and 4 pixels down, blurred by 8 pixels, with no spread and 20% opacity, so it reads as a soft grey rather than a black edge.

faq.q: What order do the values go in?
faq.a: Inset first if you want an inner shadow, then the x offset, y offset, blur radius, spread radius and colour. The tool writes them in that order.

faq.q: Why does it refuse a negative blur?
faq.a: A negative blur radius is not valid CSS, so the browser would drop the whole declaration. Offsets and spread may be negative; blur may not.

faq.q: What does spread actually change?
faq.a: It grows the shadow shape before the blur is applied. A positive spread makes the shadow larger than the element, a negative spread shrinks it, which is how you get a shadow on one side only.

faq.q: Can I use a colour name instead of hex?
faq.a: This tool takes hex so it can convert it to rgba and apply the opacity slider. With a named colour there is no separate alpha value to adjust.

faq.q: Where do I paste the result?
faq.a: Inside a rule, for example .card { box-shadow: 2px 4px 8px 0px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.2); }. The declaration is exactly what you copy.

color-palette-generator.title: Color palette generator
color-palette-generator.desc: Enter a hex colour to get five swatches: two tints mixed with white, the base, and two shades mixed with black, with hex and rgb values.
color-palette-generator.lede: Type a hex colour and the tool mixes it with white and black to give five swatches with both hex and rgb values, ready to copy.
color-palette-generator.how: Every swatch is a straight mix of the base colour with either white or black, done per channel with the same formula: new channel equals the base channel multiplied by one minus the mix amount, plus the target channel multiplied by the mix amount, rounded to a whole number. Two tints use white at 50% and 25%, the third swatch is the base untouched, and two shades use black at 25% and 50%. Because only the distance to white or black changes, the hue stays in the same family and the swatches step evenly in lightness, which is what a palette needs. Three-digit hex is expanded first, and values outside 0 to 255 cannot occur because the mix is clamped.
color-palette-generator.example: For #336699 the channels are 51, 102 and 153. The 50% tint gives 51 × 0.5 + 255 × 0.5 = 153, 178.5 and 204, which rounds to #99B3CC. The 25% tint gives #668CB3, the base is #336699, the 25% shade gives #264D73 and the 50% shade gives #1A334D. Each swatch also reports its rgb values, for example rgb(153, 179, 204) for the first tint.

faq.q: How are the tints calculated?
faq.a: Each channel is mixed with 255 at 50% and again at 25%, then rounded. That is a straight linear blend toward white, not a change of hue or saturation.

faq.q: Why exactly five swatches?
faq.a: Two tints, the base and two shades give a usable range of contrast steps without producing colours so close together that they are indistinguishable.

faq.q: Can I paste an rgb() value?
faq.a: Only hex is accepted: three digits such as #06c or six digits such as #336699. Anything else gets a specific error message.

faq.q: Are these colours accessible together?
faq.a: Not necessarily. This tool only mixes colours; check any text and background pair with the contrast checker before using it for text.

faq.q: Does the base colour stay in the list?
faq.a: Yes, it is the middle swatch, unchanged, so you can compare every tint and shade against it.

password-strength-checker.title: Password strength checker
password-strength-checker.desc: Estimate a password's entropy from its length and the character classes it uses. Runs in the page and is never stored, sent or logged.
password-strength-checker.lede: Type a password to see how many bits of entropy it represents, which character classes it uses, and how the estimate is calculated.
password-strength-checker.how: The estimate assumes every character was picked at random from the set the password draws on. That set, the pool, is the sum of the classes in use: 26 for lowercase, 26 for uppercase, 10 for digits, 32 for punctuation and one more for a space. Entropy is the length multiplied by the base-two logarithm of the pool size, which is the same as length × log(pool) ÷ log(2). The bar shows the result against 128 bits and the labels use fixed thresholds printed with the result: under 28 very weak, under 36 weak, under 60 fair, under 80 strong, 80 and above very strong. This is an estimate, not a measurement and not a prediction of how long a guess would take.
password-strength-checker.example: For Tr0ub4dor&3 the length is 11 and all four classes are present, so the pool is 26 + 26 + 10 + 32 = 94. The base-two logarithm of 94 is 6.5546 bits per character, and 11 × 6.5546 = 72.10 bits, which the tool labels strong because it is between 60 and 80.

faq.q: Is this a crack-time estimate?
faq.a: No. It reports entropy on the assumption that each character was chosen uniformly at random from the pool. A password made of two dictionary words has far less real entropy than its character count suggests.

faq.q: Why 32 symbols?
faq.a: That is the count of punctuation characters on a standard US keyboard layout. A space adds one more to the pool because it is a separate, usually unexpected character.

faq.q: What do the labels mean?
faq.a: They are this tool's fixed bands: under 28 bits very weak, 28 to 35 weak, 36 to 59 fair, 60 to 79 strong, and 80 or more very strong.

faq.q: Is my password sent anywhere or stored?
faq.a: No. It is read in this page, used for the arithmetic and never written to storage, a cookie, the URL or the console. Reloading loses it immediately.

faq.q: Does a long passphrase score well?
faq.a: Yes, if it mixes classes. A 20-character phrase in lowercase letters only gives 20 × log₂(26) = 94.01 bits, while a short password using all four classes gains from the larger pool.

favicon-generator.title: Favicon generator
favicon-generator.desc: Turn one image into favicon PNGs at 16, 32, 48, 180, 192 and 512 pixels, drawn on a canvas in your browser. Nothing is uploaded.
favicon-generator.lede: Choose an image and the tool draws it into six square PNG files, with a download button for each size and a progress bar as it works.
favicon-generator.how: The image is decoded by the browser first, and an image that fails to decode is reported instead of producing blank files. Favicons must be square, so the largest centred square of your image is used and the rest is cropped away. That square is then drawn into a canvas at each size in the list, using the canvas smoothing settings, and each canvas is exported as a PNG blob. Every size gets its own download button, and the file size of each PNG is shown next to it. Uploads are capped at 5 MB and empty files are rejected, because an empty file cannot be decoded. The image never leaves the page: the canvas work happens in your browser.
favicon-generator.example: Upload a 1024 by 1024 PNG and the tool produces six files: 16, 32, 48, 180, 192 and 512 pixels square. Because the source is already square there is no crop, and the 512 file is exactly 512 by 512 pixels. A 1000 by 800 image would first be cropped to the centre 800 by 800 square, then scaled down to those same six sizes.

faq.q: Which size do I need?
faq.a: 16 and 32 for browser tabs, 48 for Windows shortcuts, 180 for the Apple touch icon, 192 for Android home screens and 512 for stores and web app manifests. The page produces all six.

faq.q: Why was my image cropped?
faq.a: A favicon has to be square, so the largest centred square is taken and the edges are dropped. Nothing is stretched, which would distort the artwork.

faq.q: Is my image uploaded?
faq.a: No. It is read into an image element and drawn on a canvas inside the page. There is no network request and no storage.

faq.q: Which input formats work?
faq.a: Any format the browser can decode, which usually means PNG, JPEG, WebP, GIF and SVG. The output is always PNG regardless of the input.

faq.q: Can it make an .ico file?
faq.a: No. It writes PNG files, which browsers and web app manifests accept for these sizes. An .ico is a separate container format and is not produced here.

html-to-markdown.title: HTML to Markdown converter
html-to-markdown.desc: Paste HTML to get Markdown: headings, bold, italics, links, lists, quotes, code and tables, written as text only. Nothing is executed.
html-to-markdown.lede: Paste an HTML fragment and the tool writes the Markdown equivalent as text you can copy, with tags turned into headings, links, lists and code blocks.
html-to-markdown.how: The HTML is parsed with the browser's DOMParser into a separate, inert document, so scripts in the input never run and images never load. Elements are then walked in order and each one is translated: headings become hash marks, strong and bold become double asterisks, italics become single asterisks, links become brackets with the address in parentheses, images become an exclamation mark and alt text, lists become dashes or numbers, quotes get a leading angle bracket and pre blocks become fenced code. Attributes other than a link or image address are dropped because Markdown has nowhere to put them. Whitespace is collapsed, then blank lines are normalised so the output reads as Markdown rather than a wall of text.
html-to-markdown.example:
For

Notes

Hello world and link.

  • One
  • Two
the output is four blocks: ## Notes, then Hello **world** and [link](https://YOURDOMAIN.com/x)., then a bullet for One and a bullet for Two. The heading level comes from the h2 tag, the bold text is wrapped in double asterisks, and the link keeps both its label and its address.

faq.q: Is the HTML I paste executed?
faq.a: No. It is parsed into an inert document that has no browsing context, so scripts do not run and external images are never fetched. The result is written into a textarea as plain text.

faq.q: Which elements are converted?
faq.a: Headings h1 to h6, paragraphs, strong and b, em and i, inline code, pre blocks, links, images, line breaks, horizontal rules, ordered and unordered lists, blockquotes and simple tables. Anything else keeps its text content.

faq.q: What happens to class names and styles?
faq.a: They are dropped. Markdown has no equivalent for classes, ids or inline CSS, so only the structure survives the conversion.

faq.q: Why is my table flattened?
faq.a: Cells become pipe-separated columns with a separator row after the first row. Merged cells, nested tables and captions cannot be represented in basic Markdown, so their text is kept and the structure is lost.

faq.q: Are the original line breaks kept?
faq.a: Not from the source formatting: runs of whitespace collapse into one space. Line breaks in the output come from the structure, meaning separate paragraphs, list items and br tags.
